title: Devlens Research Summary: WFP's food lifeline faces a $210 million gap
excerpt: WFP's November 2026 brief says it needs $277.7 million over 12 months and faces a $210 million gap. Rohingya food aid is funded only to April 2027.

image.alt: A Rohingya woman at a World Food Programme food distribution point stacked with sacks, Cox's Bazar
image.credit: DFID - UK Department for International Development / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

content:
The World Food Programme (WFP) in Bangladesh needs $277.7 million over the next 12 months and has a funding gap of $210 million, according to its Country Brief for November 2026, published on ReliefWeb on Friday (27 November). Its food assistance to about 1.2 million Rohingya refugees is funded only for the first four months of 2027, and without new money "food assistance pipelines are projected to face interruptions before mid-2027".

The brief is short, three pages, but it is the clearest single picture of where WFP's work in Bangladesh stands as aid budgets shrink. This summary sets out what it says and what it means for NGOs.

The source

WFP Bangladesh Country Brief, November 2026, covering October 2026. It is a WFP publication, not an independent evaluation. Its funding figures are WFP's own; its food insecurity and nutrition figures cite the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) and national surveys. Devlens has read the full brief.

Where things stand

In October WFP assisted 1.24 million people, 51.5% of them women. It distributed 287.2 tonnes of food and transferred $5.5 million in cash. Across the five-year Country Strategic Plan (2022-2027), the total requirement is $1,582.97 million and funding received is $1,362.01 million. The six-month net funding requirement is $72.49 million.

Finding 1: Rohingya food aid is safe only to April

A second tranche of United States funding, channelled through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), will support assistance to 1.2 million Rohingya refugees for only the first four months of 2027. The brief says 94% of refugees depend on humanitarian assistance to meet minimum food needs, and up to 1.29 million people are expected to need humanitarian help in 2027. Insecurity in Rakhine State continues to limit prospects for return. Devlens reported earlier that Rohingya food aid is funded until April 2027; the brief confirms that the gap after that is unfilled.

Smaller contributions are filling parts of the basket. The Republic of Korea gave $5 million for food and nutrition and fortified rice; Sweden funded 3,010 tonnes of red lentils under the Grain from Ukraine initiative. More than 240,000 refugee children received fortified biscuits in October, and over 8,800 refugee volunteers did cash-for-work on camp infrastructure and disaster risk reduction.

Finding 2: Hunger outside the camps is high

The brief repeats the IPC projection of 18.1 million people facing acute food insecurity in the September to December 2026 lean season (see Devlens' IPC story). One in four children under five is stunted and 11% are wasted; two in five households face micronutrient deficiencies. WFP lists persistent inflation, weaker purchasing power and an 82% probability of El Niño in 2026-2027 as risks to food production, prices and livelihoods.

Finding 3: WFP is shifting towards government systems

Much of WFP's national work is now technical support to government programmes rather than direct delivery. With WFP support, the Government Primary School Feeding Programme reached more than 3 million of the 10.61 million children in government primary schools, in 150 of 503 upazilas. A separate US Department of Agriculture-funded McGovern-Dole programme fed over 31,900 students in Madhabpur upazila, Habiganj.

The government, with WFP and partners, launched Shock-Responsive Social Protection Standard Operating Procedures, meant to let the state scale up support quickly in a crisis through social protection systems that reach about 36.3 million people. WFP and the Insurance Development and Regulatory Authority (IDRA) agreed to develop Bangladesh's first Climate Risk Insurance and Disaster Risk Financing Policy. WFP and GAIN launched a Fortification Alliance of Bangladesh with more than 150 members, and WFP supported landslide volunteer guidelines, lightning preparedness procedures and the Early Warnings for All roadmap.

Finding 4: A new country plan is coming

WFP is drafting a new five-year Country Strategic Plan aligned with the government's Five-Year Framework, and is extending the current plan through 2027 to bridge the gap. The new plan is being aligned with Bangladesh's graduation from Least Developed Country status and the next UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework.

What it means for the development sector

  • Rohingya response partners should plan for a possible food pipeline break from May 2027. Cooperating partners that distribute WFP food or run nutrition sites face the same cliff, and any cut in rations will raise malnutrition and protection risks already flagged by UNHCR.
  • National NGOs in social protection may find more work in targeting, grievance handling and shock response as government systems take over from direct aid. The new SOPs and the Family Card rollout (see today's story) are where that work will sit.
  • Climate and disaster programmes should follow the climate risk insurance policy with IDRA, which could change how anticipatory cash is funded.
  • Donors face a choice between short tranches that keep the camps fed for months at a time and multi-year funding that lets partners plan.

Limits of the evidence

The brief is WFP's own reporting and does not show results, only activities and funding. It gives no breakdown of the $210 million gap between the Rohingya response and national programmes, and does not say how large a ration cut would be if money does not come. The El Niño probability is a forecast. The school feeding reach figure comes from a government programme WFP supports, not WFP delivery alone.

The bottom line

WFP has enough money to feed the Rohingya camps until April 2027 and a $210 million hole after that. Outside the camps, it is moving from handing out food to helping government systems respond faster. Both shifts put more weight on how well national programmes and the remaining donors fill the space WFP is leaving.

Sources

  • WFP via ReliefWeb: WFP Bangladesh Country Brief, November 2026, 27 November 2026
